descs.t: Ukraine's General Staff says Russian forces used the humanitarian ceasefire in occupied Oleshky to rotate troops and replenish ammunition, and Sky News drone footage appears to show heavy equipment moving in during the pause. The mission evacuated nearly 800 people. We go through what the footage shows and what happened when the truce ended.

A humanitarian pause in occupied Oleshky got nearly 800 civilians out, but Ukraine's General Staff says Russia used the same window to reinforce, and Sky News footage appears to back that up. Reports say Kherson was struck again soon after the truce ended. We look at why Ukrainian soldiers warned this would happen and what it means for any future deal.

Ukraine agreed to a pause so civilians could escape Oleshky. According to Ukraine's General Staff and Sky News drone footage, Russian forces used it to bring in armor, troops and ammunition, and Kherson came under fire again right after. We break down the evidence and what it says about trusting Putin's word on any ceasefire.

intro.plain: A humanitarian ceasefire in occupied Oleshky just ended. It got nearly 800 people out. But Ukraine's General Staff says Russian forces used the pause to rotate troops and restock ammunition, and Sky News drone footage appears to show heavy equipment moving in. So what does the footage actually show? Chat, does this make you more or less open to ceasefire talks?
intro.mid: The Oleshky humanitarian pause saved nearly 800 civilians, and according to Ukraine, Russia used every hour of it to reinforce. Sky News drone footage appears to show armor rolling in, and reports say Kherson was hit again as soon as it ended. Ukrainian soldiers warned this would happen. Chat, I want to know: should Ukraine ever agree to a pause like this again?
intro.bold: Ukraine paused the fighting so civilians could get out of Oleshky. Russia, according to Ukraine's General Staff, used the pause to move in tanks, troops and ammo, and it is on camera. Then Kherson got hit again. This is what a ceasefire with Putin looks like. Chat, be honest: can anyone trust a deal with Moscow after this?

hook.plain: Nearly 800 people were evacuated from Oleshky during a humanitarian pause. Ukraine says Russia used the same pause to reinforce. Here is what the drone footage shows.
hook.mid: A ceasefire meant to save civilians, and drone footage that appears to show Russian armor moving in during it. Here is what happened in Oleshky, and why it matters for any deal.
hook.bold: They stopped shooting so civilians could escape. Russia, Ukraine says, used it to bring in tanks and ammo. Here is the footage, and what it says about Putin's word.

descs.t: The US Supreme Court has rejected the Trump administration's emergency request to make California set aside roughly 20,000 mail ballots from voters the federal government flagged as likely noncitizens. A federal judge, James Boasberg, had already blocked the Justice Department's demand. We walk through what was asked, what the courts decided and what it means for Tuesday's count.

The Supreme Court turned down the Trump administration's bid to have California sideline about 20,000 mail ballots the Justice Department says may have come from noncitizens. Critics of the request say the federal data is flawed, while the administration says noncitizen voting dilutes lawful votes. We look at both claims and what the ruling settles before the midterms.

The Trump administration wanted roughly 20,000 California mail ballots set aside as likely noncitizen votes, and the Supreme Court said no. A US attorney says 34 noncitizens in California have now been charged with illegally registering and voting, while Gavin Newsom calls the federal push intimidation. We break down the fight over who gets counted on the eve of the vote.

intro.plain: Big ruling right before Tuesday. The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's emergency request to make California set aside about 20,000 mail ballots the federal government flagged as likely noncitizen votes. A federal judge had already blocked the same demand. So those ballots get counted. Chat, do you think the court got this right?
intro.mid: The Supreme Court just said no to the Trump administration on California's ballots. Washington wanted roughly 20,000 mail ballots from suspected noncitizens set aside; the court refused, after Judge Boasberg also blocked the Justice Department. Critics say the federal list is flawed, the administration says noncitizen votes dilute lawful ones. Chat, which side has the stronger case?
intro.bold: Twenty thousand flagged ballots, and the Supreme Court says California counts them all. The Trump administration called them likely noncitizen votes, a US attorney says 34 noncitizens in the state have already been charged, and Gavin Newsom calls the push intimidation. This is a fight over who gets to decide an election. Chat, where do you stand?

hook.plain: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to set aside roughly 20,000 California mail ballots. The court refused. Here is what was asked, why it failed and what happens to those ballots.
hook.mid: Two courts, one answer: California keeps counting about 20,000 ballots the federal government flagged as likely noncitizen votes. Here is the case each side made and what the ruling settles.
hook.bold: Thirty four noncitizens charged, 20,000 ballots flagged, and the Supreme Court still says count them. Here is the ballot fight in California the night before the country votes.

descs.t: Michigan Senate race: Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens has endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, the candidate who beat her in the primary. Former Congressman Hansen Clarke has also backed Rogers, and the polls disagree on who leads going into Tuesday. We walk through the endorsements, the reaction and the latest polls.

Michigan's Senate race between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers was upended when Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed the Republican and members of her own staff resigned. An Emerson poll has El-Sayed ahead 51.2% to 45.2%, while at least one other poll shows Rogers in front. We look at whether the crossover endorsements can move votes on Election Day.

Michigan Democrats are turning on Haley Stevens after she endorsed Republican Mike Rogers against Abdul El-Sayed, and her own staff resigned in protest. Reports say three Michigan Democrats have now backed Rogers, and Trump has offered Stevens a spot in the Republican Party. We break down what this revolt means for the Senate seat and for the Democrats.

intro.plain: Michigan votes on Tuesday, and the Senate race has been turned upside down. Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the primary to Abdul El-Sayed, has endorsed Republican Mike Rogers, and members of her staff resigned over it. The polls disagree on who leads. So tell me in the chat: does an endorsement like this change your vote, or not?
intro.mid: The night before Michigan votes, Democrats are fighting each other. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over her own party's nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, and former Congressman Hansen Clarke followed. Emerson has El-Sayed at 51.2 to 45.2, another poll has Rogers ahead. This seat could decide who controls the Senate. Chat, who do you think takes Michigan?

Trump offered her a spot in the Republican Party, reports say. Is this courage or betrayal? Chat, tell me where you stand.

hook.mid: Haley Stevens endorsed the Republican, and her own staff resigned. One day before Michigan votes, here is what that split could mean for Abdul El-Sayed, Mike Rogers and control of the Senate.
hook.bold: Days ago she was said to be voting for El-Sayed. Now Haley Stevens is campaigning for Mike Rogers, and Michigan Democrats are in open revolt. Here is how it happened and what it could cost them.

A Tucker Carlson post claiming Trump could be days from a nuclear strike on Iran spread to tens of millions, and critics from Laura Loomer to Hans Mahncke call it a hoax timed for the midterms. Several outlets report Trump clashing with Netanyahu over a renewed attack on the Islamic Republic. We look at who is saying what and why it matters now.

Tucker Carlson says Trump is days from nuking Iran on Netanyahu's orders, and the Islamic Republic's foreign ministry jumped on it. Meanwhile Axios says Netanyahu wants the regime hit right after Tuesday. We cut through the panic, look at what the reports actually say, and ask what pressure on the regime should look like.

Axios separately reports Netanyahu is pressing Trump to strike right after Tuesday's midterms. And Trump says some people are angry he did not completely annihilate the regime. So what is reported and what is just claimed? Chat, do you believe Tucker's sources on this one?

With 7.7 million early votes in, Texas heads into Tuesday with a Senate race the polls cannot agree on: Trafalgar has Ken Paxton up 0.6, YouGov has James Talarico up 4. The governor's race between Greg Abbott and Gina Hinojosa also looks close in some polls. We look at where Texas really stands.

Texas turned out in near presidential numbers before Election Day, and Ken Paxton's Senate race against James Talarico is within a point in one final poll. Democrats talk about flipping the state, Republicans say Latino men are sticking with Trump. We break down the early vote and what it means for Tuesday.

President Trump says Chuck Schumer and Marc Elias should be held responsible for the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot, while one poll shows Peltola and Sullivan tied at 50 percent. We look at how a duplicate name could matter under ranked choice.

Two men named Dan Sullivan are on Alaska's Senate ballot, a court just tossed the DOJ's attempt to step in, and Trump calls it election fraud at the highest level. With the race tied in one poll, every confused ballot could count. We break down the fight, the appeal, and whether voters can trust the result.

descs.t: Two oil tankers exploded after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, according to an IRGC spokesperson. The Islamic Republic now says it could reopen the strait within 48 hours if the US meets its demands, which reports say include ending the US naval blockade. We walk through the blasts, the regime's conditions and the talks in Doha.

The IRGC says two oil tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and within a day the Islamic Republic was offering to reopen the strait if the US meets seven conditions. Its negotiators have left Doha talks with Qatari mediators, and a draft proposal is reportedly circulating. We look at what the regime is demanding and what it is using as leverage.

Two oil tankers exploded on mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the IRGC says, and now the Islamic Republic says the strait stays shut until the US lifts sanctions and ends its naval blockade. The regime is holding the world's oil lane as a bargaining chip. We break down its seven conditions and why pressure, not concessions, is the answer.

intro.plain: Two oil tankers have exploded in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting mines, according to an IRGC spokesperson. At the same time the Islamic Republic says it could reopen the strait within 48 hours if the US meets its demands, including ending the naval blockade. Talks in Doha have broken up for now. Chat, do you think Washington should take this offer?
intro.mid: Mines in Hormuz and an offer in the same breath. The IRGC says two tankers hit mines, and the Islamic Republic now says the strait can reopen within 48 hours if the US meets seven conditions, starting with the naval blockade. Its negotiators have left Doha. That is leverage, not diplomacy. Chat, is the regime negotiating or threatening?
intro.bold: Two tankers blown up on mines in Hormuz, by the IRGC's own account, and now the regime wants a reward for reopening the strait. Lift the sanctions, end the blockade, meet seven conditions, or the world's oil lane stays shut. That is a ransom note. Chat, should the US give the Islamic Republic a single thing?
